INSIGHTS.title: What the new arbitration rules mean for you
INSIGHTS.author: Elena Russo
INSIGHTS.excerpt: Faster timelines, tighter costs and new powers for tribunals — here is what changes for businesses in a dispute.
takeaways: Most arbitrations must now finish within 12 months of the tribunal being formed.
Emergency relief is available before the full tribunal is appointed.
Review the arbitration clause in your key contracts this quarter.

body.p: Arbitration was meant to be the faster, cheaper alternative to court. Over the years it often became neither. The latest rules try to bring it back on track — and they affect almost every commercial contract you have signed.

Tribunals are now expected to deliver an award within twelve months of being formed, with a six-month extension only by consent. Delays without reason can affect the arbitrators' fees, which gives everyone a strong incentive to keep things moving.

If you need urgent protection — to stop an asset being sold, for example — you can now ask an emergency arbitrator before the main tribunal is even in place. That closes a gap that previously pushed parties back to court.

body.quote: A well-drafted clause today saves months of argument tomorrow.

body.p: Look at the dispute clauses in your major supply, distribution and partnership agreements. Check the seat, the institution and the number of arbitrators. Small fixes now can make a big difference if a dispute ever arises.

INSIGHTS.title: Five clauses every founder should read twice
INSIGHTS.author: Daniel Whitmore
INSIGHTS.excerpt: Term sheets move fast. These five clauses decide who really controls your company — read them slowly.
takeaways: Liquidation preferences decide who gets paid first on an exit.
Vesting protects the company if a co-founder leaves early.
Never sign a term sheet without understanding the veto rights.

body.p: Fundraising is exciting, and term sheets are usually short. But a few lines in that document will shape your company for years. Here are the five we ask every founder to read twice.
This decides how money is shared when the company is sold. A simple 1x non-participating preference is standard; anything more aggressive deserves a careful conversation.
Investors often ask founders to re-vest their shares. It feels uncomfortable, but it also protects you if a co-founder walks away in year one.
Protective provisions let investors block certain decisions. Make sure the list is limited to genuinely major events, not day-to-day operations.

body.quote: The shortest clauses often carry the longest consequences.

body.p: Broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution is founder-friendly; full ratchet is not. And check whether the option pool is created before or after the investment — it changes your real valuation.

INSIGHTS.title: Buying property? Check these documents first
INSIGHTS.author: Rohan Malhotra
INSIGHTS.excerpt: A beautiful home can hide an ugly title. These documents tell you whether the seller can really sell.
takeaways: Ask for 30 years of title documents, not just the latest sale deed.
Check the encumbrance certificate for loans and mortgages.
For new projects, confirm RERA registration and approvals.

body.p: Most property disputes we see could have been avoided with a few days of document checks before signing. Here is the short list we review for every client.
The seller's sale deed is only the last link. We trace ownership back thirty years to make sure every transfer was valid and registered.
This shows whether the property is mortgaged or tied up in any registered claim. A clean certificate is essential before you pay a deposit.

body.quote: If a document is missing, the time to ask is before you pay — not after.

body.p: For apartments and new projects, check the sanctioned plan, the occupancy certificate and RERA registration. They protect you if the builder delays possession.

INSIGHTS.title: Custody and care: a calm guide
INSIGHTS.author: Priya Kapoor
INSIGHTS.excerpt: When parents separate, children need stability most. How custody decisions are made — and how to keep them calm.
takeaways: Courts decide custody based on the child's welfare above all else.
Shared parenting plans are increasingly common.
Mediation usually reaches a workable plan faster than litigation.

body.p: Separation is hard on everyone, and hardest on children. The law's starting point is simple: what is best for the child. Everything else follows from that.
Judges consider the child's age, their routine, schooling, health and, for older children, their own wishes. Neither parent starts with an automatic advantage.
Many families now agree on shared arrangements — weekdays with one parent, weekends or holidays with the other — so the child keeps a strong bond with both.

body.quote: The best custody plan is the one both parents can actually live with.

body.p: A mediated agreement is private, quicker and usually lasts longer, because both parents helped write it. We recommend trying it first wherever it is safe to do so.

INSIGHTS.title: Compliance calendars that actually work
INSIGHTS.author: Ananya Rao
INSIGHTS.excerpt: Missed filings cost money and credibility. A simple calendar — owned by one person — fixes most of it.
takeaways: List every filing once, with its owner and deadline.
Set reminders 30 and 7 days before each due date.
Review the calendar every quarter as rules change.

body.p: Most compliance failures are not about bad intentions. They are about a deadline nobody owned. A good calendar solves that with very little effort.
Write down every recurring obligation: tax filings, ROC returns, licence renewals, board meetings and policy reviews. One list, one place.
A task with two owners has none. Name one person for each filing and a backup for holidays.

body.quote: Compliance is a habit, not an emergency.

body.p: Rules change. A short quarterly review — fifteen minutes with your advisor — keeps the calendar accurate and your company out of trouble.

INSIGHTS.title: Inside a winning appeal
INSIGHTS.author: Sophia Laurent
INSIGHTS.excerpt: Appeals are not a second trial. Winning one means finding the precise point where the first decision went wrong.
takeaways: An appeal reviews legal errors, not the whole case again.
Strict time limits apply — act quickly after a judgment.
Clear, focused written arguments matter most.

body.p: Clients often see an appeal as a chance to tell their story again. In reality, an appellate court asks a narrower question: did the lower court make a mistake that changed the outcome?
We read the judgment line by line, alongside the evidence, looking for a misapplied law, an ignored document or a finding with no basis in the record.
Strong appeals argue two or three points well rather than ten points weakly. Judges respond to clarity.

body.quote: In an appeal, less argument often wins more.

body.p: Limitation periods for appeals are short. If you have received an unfavourable judgment, speak to a lawyer within days, not weeks.

INSIGHTS.title: Due diligence, the Lexora way
INSIGHTS.author: Vikram Sethi
INSIGHTS.excerpt: Due diligence is not a box to tick. Done well, it changes the price, the terms — and sometimes the decision.
takeaways: Agree the scope before you start, so effort goes where risk is.
Red-flag reports are more useful than long summaries.
Findings should feed directly into the contract.

body.p: Whether you are buying a company, investing in one or taking on a major partner, due diligence tells you what you are really getting. Here is how we approach it.
We agree with you upfront which risks matter most for this deal — litigation, tax, property, employees or regulatory — and focus there.
You get a short report that ranks issues by impact, with a clear recommendation for each. Long appendices are available, but the decisions sit on the first page.

body.quote: Good diligence doesn't just find problems — it prices them.

body.p: Every serious finding becomes a warranty, an indemnity, a price adjustment or a condition before closing. That is where diligence earns its fee.
